strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: improving finite-length quaternary codes for insertion, deletion, and substitution errors. Using learned embeddings to guide codebook construction is an interesting application.

Algorithm 1 removes neighbors using exact Levenshtein distance. As written, this guarantees minimum distance at least three and therefore a valid single-error-correcting codebook, independently of embedding accuracy.

Table 1 demonstrates consistent improvements over random greedy selection across ten runs. At length 11, the best codebook increases from 31,142 to 36,368 codewords, achieving a rate of approximately 68.9%. The original-versus-revised loss ablation also helps isolate the modification's contribution.

Table 2 provides substantial empirical decoding evidence, including zero observed failures in 100 million trials with four retrieved neighbors. A source-code link is provided, and the synthetic-data experiments raise no apparent material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: The central justification for the search criterion is incorrect or unsupported. Batch normalization does not make embeddings multivariate Gaussian. Consequently, the Gaussian density score is a heuristic whose relationship to actual edit-neighborhood cardinality needs measurement. The binary t-SNE visualization does not establish this relationship for the quaternary experiments. Furthermore, choosing low-degree candidates greedily does not guarantee a maximum-cardinality codebook.

The comparisons do not sufficiently establish the contribution over existing search methods. Random selection is the only substantive construction-search baseline; comparisons with lexicographic selection, exact or approximate neighborhood-count ordering, and local improvement are missing. Figure 4 compares against asymptotic redundancy expressions without adequately explaining their finite-length instantiation. Given the reuse of the embedding approach from [44], stronger baselines are especially important for establishing the value of the new ranking and loss.

The repeated optimality claims exceed the evidence. Agreement with a proposed redundancy curve at short lengths supplies neither an optimality certificate nor a matching converse. At length 11, the reported code has approximately 6.85 redundancy bits, whereas the substitution-only sphere-packing lower bound is approximately 5.09 bits. This leaves a substantial unresolved gap. The explicit acknowledgment that a proof is absent is welcome, but the abstract, contribution statements, and conclusion should reflect what is actually established.

The headline combination of guaranteed correction and linear-time decoding is unsupported. Retrieving one neighbor fails on approximately 0.3–0.9% of trials. Retrieving four neighbors performs well empirically, but the paper itself assigns quadratic verification cost to this configuration. Logarithmic expected k-d-tree search also requires assumptions that are not established for the 64-dimensional embeddings. Exhaustively checking all single-edit outcomes at these short lengths would establish reliability more directly than repeated random trials.

The decoding baseline is unnecessarily restrictive. General edit-distance hardness does not imply that single-error decoding requires scanning the entire codebook. An exact decoder can enumerate one-edit candidates and test codebook membership, or precompute correction neighborhoods. Comparisons against these alternatives, including their memory costs, are needed to substantiate the claimed efficiency advantage over exact decoding.

Reproducibility and resource reporting are incomplete in the manuscript. Important missing details include training-pair sampling, training-set size, optimization settings, convolutional configuration, treatment of variable-length inputs, hardware, and timing methodology. Training time, codebook construction time, initialization cost, and peak memory are also unreported. The repository link is helpful, but these omissions limit assessment of both replication and practical efficiency.

The motivating benefit to segmented storage remains unverified. Experiments evaluate isolated codewords corrupted by one edit; they do not establish segment-boundary recovery after insertions or deletions, outer-code overhead, or performance with multiple errors. Consequently, the measured codebook-rate gains do not yet establish improved overall storage density or reliable decoding of concatenated streams.
